answer.rationale: The 18% cost-cut mandate cannot be met by renewing with the incumbent (who refused to reopen price) or by renegotiating (rejected this cycle). Deferral is unacceptable because the contract expires in 14 days with no auto-renew, and the assembly line runs at 94% with zero buffer, so any lapse in supply is an immediate production risk. memory_c2 indicates that moving primary supply to the low-cost vendor last year cut unit cost sharply, onboarding was quick, and invoicing remained accurate — directly supporting the switch. However, memory_c1 shows the incumbent's integration stability and memory_c3 shows the value of a second source for constrained components. Because I can only execute one action this cycle, switching primary vendor achieves the mandated cost reduction; the remaining risk is delivery continuity. Verification of memory_c2 confirms whether the 'quick onboarding' was genuinely fast enough to fit within a 14-day transition and whether invoicing accuracy held under volume. The guard is that I will only commit if the verified record confirms onboarding completed inside the transition window at comparable volume. If verification fails or reveals hidden costs, fall back to deferral under month-to-month (per memory_c5 pattern) rather than a blind switch. This preserves the option to add a second source next cycle per memory_c3.
